title: Trump Signs New Birthright Citizenship Orders Targeting Birth Tourism After Supreme Court Loss
excerpt: A pair of executive orders narrow who qualifies for automatic citizenship, weeks after the Supreme Court affirmed the 14th Amendment right in a landmark 6-3 ruling.
body:
• President Trump signed two executive orders on August 6 banning "birth tourism" and narrowing categories of children eligible for automatic citizenship.
  • The orders follow the Supreme Court's 6-3 ruling in Trump v. Barbara on June 30, which struck down Trump's broader attempt to end birthright citizenship as unconstitutional.
  • The new orders target children of "alien enemies," foreign government employees, and parents who pay to access U.S. birthright citizenship through birth tourism.
  • Legal scholars warn the 5-4 split on the constitutional question leaves the door open for future challenges to the 14th Amendment's citizenship guarantee.

President Donald Trump signed a pair of executive orders on August 6 in a renewed attempt to curtail birthright citizenship, weeks after the Supreme Court rejected his original, broader effort as unconstitutional in one of the most closely watched cases in decades.

"We had a very unfortunate decision in the Supreme Court concerning birthright… so we're making adjustments," Trump said during a White House signing ceremony.

The Supreme Court Ruling

On June 30, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump v. Barbara that children born in the United States — including to parents unlawfully or temporarily present — are citizens at birth under the Citizenship Clause of the 14th Amendment. The Court invalidated Executive Order 14160, which Trump signed in 2025 to deny birthright citizenship to U.S.-born children whose parents lacked citizenship or permanent residency.

https://x.com/belliott123/status/2093497310885847490

"Citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights — to freely participate in our political community. The Framers of the Fourteenth Amendment extended that promise to 'every free-born person in this land.' We keep that promise today."

— Chief Justice John Roberts, writing for the majority

Chief Justice Roberts was joined by Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, Barrett, and Jackson. Justice Kavanaugh concurred based on statutory rather than constitutional grounds, making the constitutional question a 5-4 split. Justices Thomas, Alito, and Gorsuch dissented. The ruling reaffirmed the principle established in United States v. Wong Kim Ark (1898), with Roberts noting the Court has "repeatedly understood the rule of Wong Kim Ark to guarantee citizenship to all children born in the United States."

The New Executive Orders

Trump's new orders are more narrowly tailored. The first declares certain individuals ineligible for birthright citizenship when neither parent is a citizen, covering three categories: children of "alien enemies," children of foreign government employees, and children of parents who engage in a "commercial transaction" to access birthright citizenship — including paying to ensure a mother is present in the United States to give birth.

The second order directs the State Department and Department of Homeland Security to prevent individuals from entering the country for the purpose of birth tourism.

"That practice of birth tourism is, as of the signing of this order, hereby banned," White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller said at the ceremony. "No one in the world is anymore allowed to obtain a visa for this fraudulent purpose."

The administration argues these categories "do not fall within the rule of birthright citizenship as announced by the Supreme Court," positioning the new orders as compliant with the June 30 ruling rather than defiant of it.

Legal Challenges Ahead

The American Civil Liberties Union immediately signaled it would fight the new orders. "The Supreme Court already decided this issue: Birthright citizenship is guaranteed by the Constitution," the ACLU said. "Any executive order that tries to attack birthright citizenship will meet the same fate as President Trump's last one."

Legal scholars, however, caution the constitutional question may not be as settled as the headline ruling suggests. UC Berkeley law professor Amanda Tyler, writing in a California Law Review Online column published August 27, warned that the 5-4 split on constitutionality leaves the principle vulnerable to future attack.

"Sadly, what could have — and should have — been a shining moment for the Supreme Court to hand down a unanimous decision reaffirming birthright citizenship was not meant to be," Tyler wrote. "The divided vote in Trump v. Barbara may only serve to fan the flames of a continuing national divide over who should enjoy the privileges of United States citizenship."

Birth Tourism: How Big Is the Issue?

The scale of birth tourism remains disputed. The Center for Immigration Studies estimated between 20,000 and 25,000 mothers came to the U.S. for birth tourism in a year-long period between 2016 and 2017, out of 3.6 million total U.S. births in 2025. University professors who filed a brief with the Supreme Court called the practice "an infinitesimal proportion" of American births. Trump claimed the number is in the "hundreds of thousands."

House Speaker Mike Johnson said on July 5 that he supports legislative efforts. "If there is a bill that can fix that, we'll advance that immediately," Johnson said. However, because the Supreme Court majority found the right constitutionally protected, any legislation would likely require a constitutional amendment — needing two-thirds support in both chambers of Congress and ratification by three-fourths of state legislatures.

Implications for the Diaspora

For Indian-origin families in the United States, the ongoing legal battle carries direct implications. Many Indian immigrants on temporary work visas have children born on U.S. soil who are citizens by birthright. While the current orders target birth tourism and narrower categories, the divided Supreme Court ruling and the administration's persistence signal that the boundaries of birthright citizenship will remain a contested legal question. Legal experts advise individuals with questions about their children's citizenship status to consult an immigration attorney.
